title: Functional Divergence of Upper- and Lower-Body Fat Distribution and Differences in Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease Risk and Outcomes: A Narrative Review
content: Traditional obesity risk assessment centers on body mass index (BMI); however, marked differences in cardiovascular and cerebrovascular outcomes despite comparable total adiposity suggest that the regional attributes of adipose tissue have independent explanatory value. Consistent evidence from cohort studies and Mendelian randomization (MR) shows that upper-body (abdominal/truncal) fat is positively associated with cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk, whereas lower-body (gluteofemoral/leg) fat is independently associated with reduced risk at the adipose depot volume level. In a South Indian dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) study, each 1-SD increase in android fat was associated with an odds ratio (OR) for type 2 diabetes of 6.59 (95% CI, 3.17–13.70) in men, whereas the OR for leg fat was 0.42 (95% CI, 0.24–0.74). A dose-response meta-analysis showed that each 10-cm increase in hip circumference was associated with a 10% lower risk of all-cause mortality (hazard ratio (HR), 0.90; 95% CI, 0.81–0.99); after adjustment for BMI and waist circumference, the association strengthened to an HR of 0.78 (95% CI, 0.66–0.90). Data from the UK Biobank showed that, after adjustment for BMI and waist circumference, each 1-SD increase in hip circumference was associated with a 5% lower risk of coronary heart disease (HR, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.93–0.97). A cross-cohort reclassification analysis showed that among individuals with a "normal-weight" BMI, 5% had an elevated waist circumference and 18% had an elevated waist-to-hip ratio; most of these individuals, who were not identified by BMI-based classification, had a 15%–50% increased risk of cardiovascular outcomes. A Chinese population cohort showed that dynamic changes in the weight-adjusted waist index were independently associated with cardiovascular and cerebrovascular mortality, with the group showing the largest increase having a 1.52-fold higher risk than the lowest group. Upper-body fat risk exhibited a dose-dependent pattern: a high visceral adiposity index was associated with a 55% increased risk of cardiovascular disease (risk ratio (RR), 1.55; 95% CI, 1.36–1.76). The causal signal for visceral adipose tissue (VAT) is highly sensitive to exposure definition and inferential framework. Within an MR framework using MRI-measured VAT volume and BMI adjustment, VAT had no robust effect on atherosclerotic outcomes. In contrast, observational associations of BMI-adjusted MRI-defined VAT showed a positive signal. An MR study across multiple vascular beds used MRI-derived fat depots as exposure measures. After BMI adjustment, each 1-SD increase in gluteofemoral adipose tissue (GFAT) volume was associated with 17%, 24%, and 28% lower risks of myocardial infarction, large-artery atherosclerotic stroke, and peripheral artery disease, respectively. These effects attenuated but remained significant after adjustment for lipids. In contrast, causal estimates for waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) and hip circumference were not robust in sensitivity analyses. Sex-specific MR showed that the causal association between WHR and coronary heart disease was significant in women (OR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06–1.26) but not in men. At the mechanistic level, paired chromatin landscape analysis of subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) and omental visceral adipose tissue (OVAT) showed that OVAT-specific differentially accessible regions were approximately twice as numerous as those in SAT and were enriched at promoters of cardiomyopathy-related genes. AI-driven large-scale clinical phenotyping in 101,243 patients showed that individuals positive for brown adipose tissue (BAT) had a lower prevalence of cardiovascular and psychiatric diseases. Higher BAT activity was associated with lower odds of cardiometabolic disease, and angiotensin receptor blocker use was positively associated with BAT, suggesting that BAT has preliminary druggable-target signals, although causal and hard-endpoint evidence is not yet established. A retrospective cohort of 13,530 patients undergoing PET/CT further showed that BAT positivity was independently associated with a lower incidence of cardiovascular events (P=0.018). Perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) and epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) influence arterial stiffness, ventricular remodeling, and arrhythmias through paracrine pathways adjacent to target organs. EAT volume was independently associated with new-onset atrial fibrillation (HR per 1-SD increase, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.05–1.58; still significant after adjustment for BMI and left atrial volume). The CT-accessible Fat Attenuation Index has translated the inflammatory phenotype of PVAT into a clinically deployable prognostic tool; pericoronary adipose tissue (PCAT) attenuation was significantly associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) risk (HR, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.38–1.81) and all-cause mortality (HR, 1.77), but this effect size was highly sensitive to analytical strategy. Radiomic quantification of EAT volume and the PVAT inflammatory phenotype jointly support the feasibility of opportunistic risk stratification. At the intervention level, several lines of evidence jointly support "distribution improvement" as an independent dimension for evaluating interventions beyond weight loss alone. These include CENTRAL/DIRECT-PLUS, the primary and mediation analyses of SELECT, comparisons of VAT reduction across different intervention pathways, the SUMMIT CMR substudy, the DAPA-EAT trial, and evidence on dapagliflozin and EAT. Heart failure outcomes exhibit heterogeneity by ejection fraction phenotype. A prospective cohort of 428,000 participants in the UK Biobank showed that heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) was independently associated with all adiposity measures (VAT: HR, 1.23), whereas heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) was not independently associated with adiposity measures. EAT was consistently associated with harm in HFpEF/heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) but showed a paradoxical association in HFrEF. Among patients with HFpEF, 91% had an elevated waist circumference and 85% had elevated VAT, but only 38% met the BMI criterion for obesity. The PARAGON-HF trial further showed that the prevalence of central obesity (waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) ≥0.5) in HFpEF was as high as 96%, whereas BMI-defined obesity was present in only 49%. In diabetic HFrEF, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR)-defined sarcopenic obesity was independently associated with approximately a 3-fold risk of adverse outcomes (HR, 3.03; 95% CI, 1.39–6.63). Three-dimensional deep learning segmentation of whole-body MRI has enabled direct quantification of GFAT and provided incremental discrimination of ΔAUC 0.01–0.02 beyond models already containing BMI and WHR. A sarcopenic obesity index derived from routine CMR (body weight/pectoralis major mass) in 55,768 UK Biobank CMR scans showed that each 1-SD increase was associated with a 31% higher risk of incident heart failure, a 51% higher risk of cardiovascular death, and a 37% higher risk of all-cause death. This index provides a scalable operational tool for characterizing the "fat–muscle configuration." AI-derived MRI body composition analysis further showed that, after full adjustment for BMI and waist circumference, only VAT proportion and skeletal muscle fat fraction independently provided incremental prognostic information for MACE. This suggests that opportunistic radiomic quantification is extending beyond the boundaries of circumference-based proxies. Critical benchmarking of novel body shape indices suggests that BMI combined with WHR captures nearly all body shape information relevant to cardiometabolic disease; novel indices have incremental value but are not yet sufficient to support widespread replacement of BMI + WHR. The Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) cohort showed that WHR significantly modifies the cardiovascular risk associated with lipoprotein(a) (Lp[a]): individuals with Lp(a) ≥50 mg/dL and WHR ≥90th percentile had the highest atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) incidence (35.7/1,000 person-years). The American Diabetes Association (ADA) 2026 standards and the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome guideline have incorporated distribution indicators such as waist circumference into risk stratification; the Expert Consensus on the Management of Obesity in the Elderly (2026 Edition) further provides diagnostic cutoffs for waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio in Chinese older adults. This narrative review synthesizes the above evidence, using "functional divergence" as the organizing thread.
